What was the scariest part during the cold war? Did you have any special plans in place?
How Was Life Back in The Cold War Days?

Their was a sense of dread. We were always reminded that the world could end in 30 mins. So we didn't really have a sense of a good future. I see the same thing with millennials now. When they are burdened with debt and no real job prospects.
I remember learning where our towns bomb shelters were located. My schools all head bomb shelter signs on the outside.
We were comforted with news that our city was listed as a top target. So we had that goin for us, which was nice.
Read Marzi. It's an interesting comic about a girl in communist Poland in the 80s. They messed up the English edition, though.
Did people really think that hiding under a wooden desk would really help them survive nuclear boom?
Each class had a seating plan. The dead Kid under that desk must be so and so.
Fear and misinformation everywhere. People who where afraid are easy to control. Hiding under a desk during a nuclear raid will not save you, like, at all.

At the start of each school year, we would have to have our parents sign a form, indicating whether, in the event of an attack, we should stay in the school basement, which doubled as a fallout shelter, or to immediately start walking home. My mother always checked the "start walking home" box. Back then, I thought she just wanted us home with her. When I brought up the topic as an adult, she told me that she wanted to be sure we were dead on the trip home, rather than to have to worry whether or not we were alive.
Holy shit, dude. That's both the bravest and darkest thing I've heard in a long time. Damn.

My sister and I would practice jumping into gullies on the way home, just in case we heard a bomb. I found out later that, since we were within 10 miles of New York City and the Brooklyn Navy Yard, we would just have been part of the uber crater of the NY metro area - from Connecticut to Philadelphia. My mom needn't have worried.

I was in elementary school. We did under the desk drills. We also had one where we lined up in an interior hallway, in the duck and cover position, just a row of students along both sides of the whole hallway, facing the wall and huddled over. Looking back at it, I wonder if that hallway had been built specifically for nuclear threat. It had no windows or anything, and it was huge. All the kids in the school fit in there lined up.
Not from then but in Canada we build a kickass fallout shelter. It is a museum now.

I grew up 1 mile away from the second largest drop forge press in the free world. We were a primary target. I sat in a window row in 3rd grade. In the event of a huge burning blinding flash my job was to pull down the canvas blast shade to keep the glass from exploding into the classroom. Then I was told to get under my desk. We practiced this. The rope on my shade had a knot in it so I couldn't lower it all the way. The teacher said it probably wouldn't matter because we would all probably die just the same. She said to make sure to get under our own desk so that Our parents could bury the right child. I am not kidding. I stared out those windows for weeks terrified. I read FAIL SAFE shortly after that and stole "The effects of nuclear weapons" from the school library and kept it under my bed.
Holy SHIT. We did drills in my school but we never actually talked about why we were doing them. This was at the very, very end of the Cold war period, but still. How did you cope with the fear?

This was in '72. My teacher was nearing retirement, and she was crazy. But she told us the truth. To deal with it I read everything I could about it. Thinking back if I had a kid that was reading Scientific articles about Strontium and cesium in cows milk and their effects on children, I would have been worried. Maybe my fear was manufactured, and through that fear they got my consent for the arms race, I don't know. But I remember always knowing that my grandfather worked at a primary target, and my father worked a lot in Boston, and I hoped that if there was a war, that It would happen at night.

Mutually Assured Destruction, fallout shelter signs, and living in an area of military bases, knowing that the bomb was going to take out our town first (according to our parents.)
